auxiliary_material: The authors performed complete genome sequencing using PacBio SMRT technology, phylogenetic analysis of 16S rRNA and ITS regions, and phenotypic microarray analysis to classify the bacterium as Bacillus infantis. They identified 623 potential virulence factors, including adhesins, invasins, and transporters. The study also notes the presence of unique methyltransferases and insertion sequence elements. These details support the characterization of the bacterium but are less directly relevant to the specific signaling pathway question regarding Prevotella.

remaining_gap: The supplied material does not mention Prevotella spp., the FMT-LUMINate study, or any downstream signaling pathways specific to Prevotella-induced myocarditis. The mechanism described is specific to Bacillus infantis and cardiac myosin mimicry. There is no information on whether Prevotella uses a similar mimicry strategy or distinct metabolites to activate T cells in the context of the FMT-LUMINate research.
useful_material: This study identifies a specific molecular mimicry mechanism where Bacillus infantis (strain NRRL B-14911) induces autoimmune myocarditis. The authors found that an epitope (BAC 25-40) from the bacterial allantoate amidohydrolase (AAH) protein shares sequence homology with cardiac myosin heavy chain alpha (Myhc-α 334-352). Active immunization with this epitope induced myocarditis in A/J mice by generating cardiac-reactive T cells. The study provides genomic evidence of virulence factors and confirms the conservation of this mimicry epitope. This serves as a concrete example of a bacterium inducing myocarditis via antigen-specific T cell cross-reactivity, which parallels the type of mechanism (antigen/metabolite -> T cell subset) sought in the gap question, albeit for a different bacterial species.
